questions.stem: Feminist literary criticism focuses mainly on:
options: how texts reflect class conflict and the control of economic resources
how a text's words create unity through irony, paradox and tension
how colonised peoples are represented by writers from imperial nations
how texts represent women, gender and patriarchal power
questions.explanation: Feminist criticism examines how gender is constructed and how texts reinforce or resist male dominance. Class conflict and economic power are the central concerns of Marxist criticism.

questions.stem: A Marxist reading of a text would focus mainly on:
options: the representation of gender and the experiences of women
class, economic power and the ideology that sustains them
the unconscious desires and anxieties of the characters
the relationship between human beings and the natural world
questions.explanation: Marxist criticism asks who holds economic power in a text and how its ideas make that power seem natural. Unconscious desires are the territory of psychoanalytic criticism.

questions.stem: Postcolonial criticism examines:
options: the formal unity of a poem, setting aside history and biography altogether
the stable binary oppositions that structure every narrative in a culture
the effects of colonisation and how the colonised are represented
the reader's personal response as they move through a text line by line
questions.explanation: Postcolonial critics read texts for the power relations of empire, including how colonised peoples are depicted, silenced or given voice. Setting aside history to study formal unity is the method of New Criticism.

questions.stem: Psychoanalytic criticism, drawing on Freud, reads texts for:
options: the representation of nature and environmental damage
the documents of the period read alongside the literary text
repressed desires, fears and conflicts expressed indirectly
the economic conditions of the society that produced them
questions.explanation: Psychoanalytic readings treat images, dreams, slips and patterns as signs of what characters, or texts, cannot openly express. Reading non-literary documents of the period beside the text is the method of New Historicism.

questions.stem: Ecocriticism studies:
options: the conventions of a genre and how individual texts follow them
the relationship between literature and the natural environment
the economic relationships between social classes in a text
how readers' expectations shape the meaning they make of a text
questions.explanation: Ecocritics examine how texts represent nature, landscape and environmental change, and the values those representations carry. The role of readers' expectations belongs to reader-response criticism.

questions.stem: Reader-response criticism holds that a text's meaning is:
options: found only by studying the economic system of the author's society
contained entirely within the text and identical for all readers
created in the interaction between the reader and the text
fixed permanently by the author's intentions at the time of writing
questions.explanation: Reader-response critics focus on how readers make meaning as they read, so different readers may legitimately respond differently. The view that meaning is contained wholly in the text's words is closer to New Criticism.

questions.stem: New Criticism, influential in the mid-20th century, emphasised:
options: close reading of the text itself, attending to irony, paradox and tension
the author's biography as the key to unlocking the meaning of a text
the reader's emotional response as the true location of a text's meaning
the political and economic history that produced the text in the first place
questions.explanation: New Critics treated the poem as a self-contained object whose meaning lies in its language and form, setting aside biography and history. Making the reader's response the location of meaning was the position of reader-response critics.

questions.stem: Queer theory examines how texts:
options: construct sexuality and gender, and unsettle heteronormative norms
construct social class through the ownership of land, money and labour
represent the effects of colonisation on peoples and their cultures
represent the natural environment and humanity's place within it
questions.explanation: Queer theory questions the idea that heterosexuality and fixed gender identities are natural norms, and reads texts for how they police or unsettle those norms. Land, money and labour are Marxist concerns.

questions.stem: New Historicism, associated with Stephen Greenblatt, reads a literary text:
options: as an expression of timeless human truths shared by readers in every era
beside non-literary documents of its time, to show its part in the workings of power
in isolation from history, since the words on the page contain all of its meaning
as the record of the author's unconscious desires, revealed through recurring images
questions.explanation: New Historicists place a play or novel beside sermons, legal records and travel writing of its period, treating literature as part of a culture's circulation of power. Reading in isolation from history is what New Criticism did.

questions.stem: Roland Barthes, in 'The Death of the Author' (1967), argued that:
options: authors should write anonymously so that readers are not distracted by fame
a text dies once its author does, and so cannot be interpreted afterwards
a text's meaning is not fixed by its author's intentions but made in reading
only biographical research can reveal what a text truly means to its readers
questions.explanation: Barthes rejected the idea that the author is the final authority on meaning, declaring that 'the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author'. The 'death' is a metaphor for the author's loss of authority, not a claim about anonymity.

questions.stem: A student argues that a poem cannot be about loss because the poet said in an interview it was 'just about a walk'. A New Critic would object that the student is:
options: committing the affective fallacy by confusing the poem with its emotional effect on readers
reading the poem in its context of production rather than in its context of reception
applying a postcolonial perspective to a poem that has nothing to say about empire
committing the intentional fallacy by letting the poet's stated intention override the text
questions.explanation: Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'intentional fallacy' holds that a poem's meaning lies in the text, so an author's comment cannot settle it. The affective fallacy, their other term, concerns judging a poem by its emotional effect, which is not what the student does.

questions.stem: A critic organises a reading of a novel around oppositions such as city/country and reason/passion, then argues that the novel's language undermines the very hierarchy between these terms. The critic is moving from:
options: a deconstructive reading of binaries to a structuralist identification of them
a Marxist reading of class to a psychoanalytic reading of desire
a reader-response approach to a New Historicist approach
a structuralist identification of binaries to a deconstructive reading of them
questions.explanation: Structuralism identifies the binary oppositions that organise meaning; deconstruction shows how a text unsettles the hierarchy those binaries assume. Undermining comes after identifying, so the order is from structuralist to deconstructive.

questions.stem: A 19th-century travel narrative describes an Eastern city as timeless, sensual and irrational, in contrast to the narrator's 'rational' homeland. Drawing on Edward Said, a critic would describe this as:
options: pastoral, an idealised picture of simple rural life away from the court
magic realism, the calm narration of marvels in an everyday setting
metafiction, a text that keeps drawing attention to its own artifice
Orientalism, the West's construction of the East as its inferior Other
questions.explanation: Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how Western writing built an image of 'the Orient' as exotic and irrational, defining the West as its rational opposite. The narrative's contrast does exactly that, which makes it a classic example.

questions.stem: Laura Mulvey's idea of the 'male gaze' describes how films often:
options: use extreme close-ups of male faces to suggest their inner emotional lives
position viewers to look at women as objects from a male viewpoint
show male characters through the eyes of a female narrator and her desires
allow viewers to identify equally with every character, whatever their gender
questions.explanation: Mulvey argued in 1975 that classical cinema's camera and narrative make women the object of a controlling male look. The concept is now applied widely in feminist readings of literature and other media.

questions.stem: Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar's The Madwoman in the Attic (1979) argued that 19th-century literature often confined women to two images:
options: the mentor and the trickster
the angel and the monster
the hero and the villain
the mother and the worker
questions.explanation: Gilbert and Gubar showed how male-authored traditions cast women as either the selfless angel or the rebellious monster, and how women writers worked within and against these images. The hero and villain are general character roles, not their feminist argument.

questions.stem: In Marxist criticism, 'ideology' refers to:
options: the deliberate lies a single character tells to deceive the others
the author's private political opinions, expressed openly in letters
the unconscious desires repressed by the characters in a narrative
beliefs that make the dominant group's interests seem natural
questions.explanation: Ideology works by passing off particular interests as common sense, so a text can carry it without any character arguing for it. A character's deliberate lies are a matter of plot, not ideology in this sense.

questions.stem: In a novel narrated by a wealthy landowner, the workers who keep his estate running are barely mentioned. A Marxist reading would most likely focus on:
options: how the estate's landscape is shaped by the cycles of the natural world
how the novel's structure follows the conventions of the country-house genre
how the silence about labour conceals the exploitation behind his comfort
how his repressed childhood fears surface in his dreams about the estate
questions.explanation: For a Marxist critic, what a text leaves unsaid can be as revealing as what it says, and the invisible workers expose the economic basis of the landowner's world. His fears and dreams would interest a psychoanalytic reader instead.

questions.stem: In a love poem, the beloved woman is described only as a list of body parts compared to jewels and flowers, and she never speaks. A feminist reading would most likely argue that the poem:
options: represents the economic exploitation of women's labour in the period
objectifies her, making her a silent object of the speaker's gaze
gives her a strong voice, because so much of the poem is devoted to her
critiques the speaker's desire by revealing his love to be false
questions.explanation: Cataloguing a woman's features, a convention called the blazon, turns her into something looked at rather than someone who sees or speaks. Being described at length is not the same as being given a voice.

questions.stem: A character repeatedly dreams of a locked room and avoids visiting his childhood home. A psychoanalytic reading would interpret these details as:
options: signs of a repressed trauma or desire surfacing indirectly
evidence of the economic conditions of his own social class
a representation of humanity's harm to the environment
conventions borrowed from the Gothic genre for suspense
questions.explanation: Psychoanalytic critics read dreams, avoidances and recurring images as the return of what has been repressed. The images may also be Gothic conventions, but that is a genre reading rather than a psychoanalytic one.

questions.stem: A pastoral poem presents the countryside as a pleasant backdrop for human leisure. An ecocritic might question the poem's:
options: metre, since pastoral poems should never use regular rhythms at all
accuracy about the price of farm produce in the period
portrayal of the beloved, whose silence objectifies her
assumption that nature exists mainly for human use and pleasure
questions.explanation: Ecocriticism examines the anthropocentric assumptions in how texts represent nature, such as treating it as scenery for people. The silence of a beloved is a feminist concern, not an ecocritical one.

questions.stem: In a novel, a poor governess is ignored at dinner by her wealthy employers. A Marxist reading would emphasise ___, whereas a feminist reading would emphasise ___.
options: her class position as a paid dependant; her limited options as a woman
her limited options as a woman; her class position as a paid dependant
her repressed desires; the economic system of the household
the house's natural setting; her limited options as a woman
questions.explanation: A Marxist reading foregrounds her economic position, a worker inside a household of owners, while a feminist reading foregrounds how her gender narrows her choices. The same scene can support both readings, which is why critical perspectives are useful.

questions.stem: Critic A argues that a poem's meaning lies in its words and their tensions. Critic B argues that the poem means what it does to each reader as they read. Critic A and Critic B are taking, respectively:
options: a New Critical and a reader-response approach
a reader-response and a New Critical approach
a Marxist and a psychoanalytic approach
a postcolonial and a New Historicist approach
questions.explanation: New Criticism locates meaning in the text's language and form, while reader-response criticism locates it in the reader's experience of reading. Swapping the two is the usual error.

questions.stem: Gayatri Spivak's essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' asks whether:
options: authors from former colonies should write in their own languages
the most marginalised colonised people can be heard on their terms
ordinary readers have the right to interpret texts without critics
minor characters in novels should be given more lines of dialogue
questions.explanation: Spivak, a postcolonial critic, argued that the subaltern, those excluded from power, are usually spoken for by others, including well-meaning Western intellectuals. The question is political and theoretical, not about dialogue in novels.

questions.stem: In a text, an 'assumption' is best defined as:
options: an idea the text takes for granted as natural or true
a claim the text argues for openly and supports with detailed evidence
a prediction a reader makes about what will happen later in the plot
a value the text openly rejects through the fate of a character
questions.explanation: Assumptions are often invisible because they are presented as common sense, which is why critical readings seek them out. A claim argued for openly is a view the text advances, not something it assumes.

questions.stem: A novel's narrator praises a self-sacrificing mother at length, while her rebellious daughter is given no voice at all. The daughter's perspective is:
options: endorsed
celebrated
foregrounded
marginalised
questions.explanation: To marginalise a perspective is to push it to the edges, denying it space or sympathy. The study design asks students to analyse how a text's views and values are endorsed, challenged and marginalised.

questions.stem: A novel spends most of its chapters celebrating a war hero's courage, but its final chapter shows him alone and haunted, forgotten by the nation that praised him. This structure most likely:
options: shows that the novel has no consistent view of war or of the hero himself
reveals that the hero was a coward all along and never fought at all
challenges the glorification of war the earlier chapters seemed to endorse
confirms the earlier chapters' celebration by adding a final, peaceful scene of rest
questions.explanation: An ending recasts what came before, so the hero's neglect exposes the hollowness of the praise. Holding contrasting attitudes in tension is a structural strategy, not inconsistency.

questions.stem: A reader who resists a text's apparent values and attends to what it marginalises is said to be reading:
options: with the grain
through intertextuality
against the grain
in medias res
questions.explanation: Reading against the grain looks for the tensions, silences and alternative views a text suppresses. Reading with the grain accepts the values the text appears to promote.

questions.stem: Knowing that a novel was written soon after a bitter civil war helps a reader interpret its obsession with divided families as:
options: a convention of romance fiction
an accident of the plot with no meaning
an image of the nation's own division
a sign that the author had no family
questions.explanation: Historical context can reveal how private stories carry public meanings, and a family split in two can stand for a divided nation. Context informs interpretation without being the only source of meaning.

questions.stem: A plausible interpretation of a text must be:
options: identical to the meaning the author has stated in letters or interviews
based on the first impression a reader forms when meeting the text
supported by textual evidence and consistent with the text as a whole
agreed upon by most published critics who have written about the text
questions.explanation: An interpretation is plausible when it can be argued from the text's details and survives contact with the rest of the text. Critics' agreement and an author's comments can inform a reading but cannot make it plausible on their own.

questions.stem: Which statement is an interpretation rather than a summary?
options: The protagonist's sister appears in the opening and the closing chapters only.
The novel suggests that ambition unchecked by empathy isolates rather than elevates.
The protagonist moves to the city in the second chapter and soon finds work at a bank.
The novel is divided into three parts, each named after a season of the year.
questions.explanation: An interpretation makes an arguable claim about what the text means. The other statements report events or features that no one would dispute, so they are observations rather than readings.

questions.stem: In developing an interpretation, 'key moments' are chosen because they:
options: come from the opening chapter, where the author states the theme
are the scenes most often quoted in summaries of the text
reveal the text's central ideas and can be closely analysed
contain the most dialogue of any scenes in the text
questions.explanation: Key moments are passages that carry the weight of a reading, where close analysis of language and form shows the interpretation at work. A passage's length of dialogue or popularity does not make it key.

questions.stem: When a text's ending is ambiguous, a strong interpretation:
options: argues for a reading with evidence while acknowledging the alternatives
ignores the ending, since ambiguous passages cannot support any claim about meaning
declares that the text has no meaning because its ending is unresolved
chooses whichever reading the student found most personally satisfying
questions.explanation: Ambiguity invites interpretation, and a sophisticated response commits to a reading while showing awareness of what else the text allows. Treating ambiguity as meaninglessness avoids the work of interpreting.

questions.stem: A student who grew up on a farm finds a novel's portrayal of farmers condescending; a classmate does not. In her interpretation, the student should:
options: avoid mentioning farmers at all, since her views on them might be biased
acknowledge how her context shapes her reading, while grounding it in evidence
abandon her reading, since a personal background makes any interpretation invalid
present her reaction as the only correct reading, since she knows farming best
questions.explanation: The study design asks students to consider their own views and values as readers; personal context can sharpen a reading if it is supported by the text. Experience alone does not make a reading correct.

questions.stem: A 1920s critic praised a novel's hero as a model of manly self-reliance; a critic writing decades later reads him as emotionally stunted by rigid gender codes. This difference best shows that:
options: interpretations are shaped by the values of the reader's own context
the earlier critic misread the novel because he lived closer to it
the novel must have been revised between the two critics' readings
only the most recent interpretation of a text can be considered valid
questions.explanation: Each critic reads from within their own era's assumptions about masculinity, so the same details yield different meanings. Recency does not make a reading valid; evidence does.

questions.stem: Which would be least appropriate as a supplementary reading for developing a second interpretation of a novel?
options: an explanation of the ideas of Marxist literary theory
a teacher's essay arguing the novel undercuts its own heroism
a review that only praises the novel as a gripping, five-star read
a scholarly article that reads the novel through postcolonial theory
questions.explanation: The study design states that a supplementary reading offering only opinion or evaluation of a text's merits is not appropriate. The others offer ideas that can enrich, challenge or contest the student's first reading.

questions.stem: After reading an ecocritical essay, a student revisits a novel and argues that its descriptions of cleared farmland, first read as signs of progress, can be seen as representing environmental loss. This illustrates:
options: the student abandoning all textual evidence in favour of a critic's opinion
a first interpretation formed before any close reading of the text
a comparison between a novel and its film adaptation
a supplementary reading prompting a second reading of the same details
questions.explanation: The second interpretation re-reads the same textual evidence through a new lens, so the details stay but their meaning shifts. The student still argues from the text; the essay changes the questions asked of it.

questions.stem: When using a critic's view in an interpretation, the most effective approach is to:
options: quote the critic at length as proof that the student's reading is correct
summarise the critic's whole essay before starting any analysis
avoid the text and discuss the critic's reputation and career
test the critic's idea against key moments, extending or qualifying it
questions.explanation: A supplementary reading should inform the student's own argument, so its ideas are applied to textual evidence and refined. Quoting a critic as an authority replaces analysis rather than enriching it.

questions.stem: A supplementary reading can 'contest' a set text's values when it:
options: argues that the text's assumptions are flawed or partial
summarises the text's plot in the order events occur
repeats the text's values in more modern language
describes the author's life without reference to the text
questions.explanation: To contest is to challenge, for instance by showing whose interests a text's values serve or what it leaves out. Restating or summarising a text does not engage with its values.

questions.stem: A student's first interpretation reads a play's heroine as a victim of fate. After a feminist supplementary reading, her second interpretation reads the heroine as constrained by patriarchy. The second interpretation is stronger if it:
options: abandons the play's text and discusses only gender in the modern world
argues that her first interpretation was worthless and should be deleted
re-reads key moments to show social constraints where she had seen fate
repeats her first interpretation, adding the critic's name for authority
questions.explanation: A second interpretation should show an enhanced understanding by applying the new lens to the same key moments, revealing what the first reading missed. It builds on the text, not away from it.

questions.stem: In an interpretation, a text 'challenges' a value when it:
options: mentions the value once in a character's speech without further comment
rewards the characters who hold the value with happiness and success
presents the value as natural, so that no character ever questions it
exposes the value's costs, such as the suffering it causes
questions.explanation: Texts challenge values by showing their consequences, through irony, outcomes or the suffering they cause. Rewarding characters who hold a value is how a text endorses it.

questions.stem: In literary criticism, 'the Other' refers to:
options: a minor character who acts as a foil to the protagonist of a novel or a play
a second interpretation of a text developed after reading a critical essay
the reader of a text, as distinct from its author and its narrator
a group constructed as different from and inferior to a dominant group, defining it by contrast
questions.explanation: Postcolonial and feminist critics use the term for how dominant groups define themselves against those they cast as alien or lesser, such as the colonised or women. A foil is a character-level contrast, not this power relation.
